question: A food-delivery app receives complaints that checkout is "too slow." A stakeholder immediately asks for fewer screens. What should the designer do first?

options.text: Remove the address and payment steps
Inspect the checkout journey and talk to users to find where and why delays happen
Add a progress animation to make waiting feel shorter
Copy the checkout flow from the most popular competitor

why: The complaint describes a symptom, not its cause. Reviewing funnel data and observing users can reveal whether the issue is slow loading, confusing fields, payment failures or something else.
takeaway: Problem framing: understand the cause before choosing a solution.

question: People using a budgeting app say, "I want to stop feeling surprised by bills." Which statement best captures the underlying Job to Be Done?

options.text: Add a calendar with more colors
Help me anticipate upcoming expenses so I can feel in control of my money
Send three push notifications every week
Add a dashboard with six new charts

why: JTBD describes the progress a person wants to make in a situation. The other options jump to specific features before clarifying the outcome.
takeaway: JTBD: focus on the progress people are trying to make, not the feature they request.

question: Your team wants to launch an AI shopping assistant. You are unsure whether shoppers trust AI recommendations. What is the most useful next step before investing in a full build?

options.text: Build the complete assistant to see what happens
List the key assumptions and run a small test of the riskiest trust assumption
Add more AI features to make the concept impressive
Ask the engineering team which model they prefer

why: Assumption mapping makes uncertainty visible. Testing the riskiest assumption early helps avoid spending heavily on a solution users may not trust.
takeaway: Riskiest assumption: test the uncertainty that could invalidate the idea.

question: During an interview about a new booking flow, which question is least leading and most likely to produce useful evidence?

options.text: You liked the new booking flow, right?
Wouldn't a one-tap booking button save you time?
Tell me about the last time you booked a similar service. What happened?
Do you agree that the old flow was confusing?

why: Asking about a recent real experience encourages concrete examples. The other questions suggest an expected answer or ask participants to agree with the interviewer.
takeaway: Ask about the last real experience, not what someone thinks they might do.

question: A team is debating two different onboarding concepts. Engineering estimates that building either version will take several weeks. What is a sensible way to learn which direction is clearer first?

options.text: Build both versions fully
Create lightweight clickable prototypes and test representative tasks with target users
Let the loudest stakeholder choose
Pick the version with the most screens

why: A prototype can test comprehension and task flow before costly implementation. It is a learning tool, not a miniature finished product.
takeaway: Prototype to learn: use the lowest-cost representation that can answer the question.

question: Analytics show that 38% of users abandon a profile form. The team knows where drop-off happens but not why. What should the designer do next?

options.text: Run usability sessions or interviews focused on the form
Increase the number of dashboard charts
Assume users dislike the brand colors
Remove every field without checking its purpose

why: Quantitative data reveals the scale and location of a problem. Qualitative research helps explain the reasons behind the behavior.
takeaway: Use quantitative research to see what is happening and qualitative research to explore why.

question: You are designing a medication reminder experience and need to understand how routines change across weekdays, weekends and travel. Which method is most suitable?

options.text: A one-time five-minute preference survey
A diary study in which participants record relevant moments over time
A card sort of navigation labels
A single hallway test of the home screen

why: A diary study captures behavior and context over time, including moments that may not be remembered accurately in a one-off interview.
takeaway: Diary study: capture experiences as they happen, across time and context.

question: You want to know whether first-time users can find and apply a discount code. What instruction should you give participants during a usability test?

options.text: Click the coupon button in the top-right corner
Apply the coupon code SAVE10 to your order
Find a way to apply this coupon to your order; please think aloud as you go
Tell us whether the coupon feature looks attractive

why: A task gives participants a goal without revealing the interface path. This lets the researcher observe discoverability and actual behavior.
takeaway: Test the task, not the UI instructions: do not tell participants where to click.

question: Interviews suggest users love a new feature, but analytics show very low repeat usage. What is the best research response?

options.text: Ignore analytics because interviews are more personal
Ignore interviews because analytics are always correct
Combine behavioral data with follow-up research to understand the gap
Announce that the feature is successful because initial feedback was positive

why: Triangulation compares different evidence sources. The mismatch is a clue worth investigating, not a reason to discard one source.
takeaway: Triangulation: combine methods or evidence sources to build a more reliable picture.

question: A team is redesigning a tool used by warehouse supervisors. Who should be prioritized for research?

options.text: People from the design team who have free time
Friends who use shopping apps
People who perform the warehouse supervisor tasks in the intended context
Any available office employees

why: Research participants should reflect the people, tasks and context relevant to the product decision. Convenience alone does not make a sample useful.
takeaway: Recruit for relevance: match participants to the target users and real context.

question: A travel app has 12 optional filters. New users say the search screen feels overwhelming. Which redesign best applies Progressive Disclosure?

options.text: Show essential filters first and place advanced filters behind "More options"
Show every filter at once
Remove all advanced filters permanently
Require users to complete every filter before searching

why: Progressive Disclosure reveals complexity when it becomes relevant. It keeps the initial experience focused without taking away advanced capabilities.
takeaway: Designer phrase: "Let's progressively disclose advanced options to keep the default experience focused."

question: A support portal asks users to remember a six-digit case number from a previous screen. How could the experience reduce memory effort?

options.text: Make the number flash briefly before hiding it
Display the case number in the current context, with a copy option
Ask users to memorize it before continuing
Replace it with a longer code

why: Recognition is easier than recall. Showing relevant information when it is needed reduces the burden on a user's memory.
takeaway: Recognition over recall: make needed choices and information visible.

question: In a shopping app, "Apply coupon" looks like ordinary body text, so people do not realize it is clickable. What change would most clearly signal the interaction?

options.text: Reduce the font size
Style it as a recognizable button or link with clear interactive treatment
Move it into a paragraph
Use a lighter gray than surrounding text

why: A signifier is a perceivable cue that communicates where or how an action can happen. A clear button or link treatment makes the affordance easier to notice.
takeaway: Signifiers: make interactive possibilities visible rather than relying on users to guess.

question: A user taps "Save" on a long form. Nothing appears to happen, so they tap repeatedly. What should the interface do?

options.text: Disable the button with no explanation
Provide a clear saving state followed by a success confirmation
Navigate away immediately, even if saving is incomplete
Change the button color randomly

why: Timely system feedback tells people that their action was received and whether it succeeded. It reduces uncertainty and repeated actions.
takeaway: Visibility of system status: keep users informed about what the system is doing.

question: A user accidentally removes an item from a task list. Which response supports recovery without interrupting every routine action?

options.text: Show a brief confirmation message with an Undo action
Permanently delete the item with no message
Require a five-step confirmation for every edit
Hide the task list after deletion

why: An Undo option offers a quick recovery path for a reversible action. This can prevent the cost and friction of excessive confirmation dialogs.
takeaway: Design for recovery: make common mistakes easy to reverse.

question: Users disagree about which items belong under "Account," "Preferences" and "Privacy." You want to learn how they naturally group the content. Which method fits?

options.text: Card sorting
A/B testing button colors
First-click testing on the current design only
A performance benchmark

why: Card sorting asks participants to organize content into groups and can reveal their mental models and useful category labels.
takeaway: Card sorting: discover how people expect information to be grouped.

question: A settings menu has been reorganized. Before designing its visual interface, you want to check whether people can find "Download my data" in the proposed hierarchy. What should you run?

options.text: A tree test using the text-only navigation structure
A color contrast audit
A five-second logo test
A diary study about daily routines

why: Tree testing evaluates whether people can find information in a proposed hierarchy without the influence of visual styling or page layout.
takeaway: Tree testing: validate findability in the structure before polishing the interface.

question: Customers say returning a product is frustrating, but the process spans the order page, courier pickup and refund status. What should the team map?

options.text: Only the return button
The end-to-end customer journey, including channels, steps and pain points
The color palette of the order page
The developer task list

why: A journey map makes the end-to-end experience visible across touchpoints. It helps teams identify issues that sit between screens or departments.
takeaway: Journey mapping: design the whole experience, not just one interface.

question: An online store has 2,000 headphones. Shoppers often know the features they need but cannot narrow the results. What would help most?

options.text: Add relevant filters such as price, connection type and noise cancellation
Randomize the result order
Hide product specifications
Show fewer products without explaining why

why: Faceted filters let people progressively narrow a large set using attributes relevant to their decision. They should use clear labels and reflect real product data.
takeaway: Faceted navigation: help users narrow large collections by meaningful attributes.

question: A new project-management account has no projects yet. Which empty state best helps a first-time user?

options.text: A completely blank page
"No data" with no next step
A short explanation of what belongs here, plus a clear "Create your first project" action
A long technical explanation of the database

why: A useful empty state explains the situation and gives the user a next step. It can turn a blank screen into guided onboarding.
takeaway: Empty-state design: explain, reassure and guide the next action.

question: On a donation page, the primary action is difficult to notice because the heading, helper text, secondary links and button all have similar visual weight. What should the designer do?

options.text: Increase the number of decorative elements
Create a clearer hierarchy using size, contrast, spacing and emphasis
Make every element bold
Remove all supporting information

why: Visual hierarchy helps people understand what is most important and what to do next. Multiple competing focal points weaken that guidance.
takeaway: Visual hierarchy: make the most important action easiest to find.

question: A product has six slightly different purple button colors across screens. The team wants consistent updates without editing each screen individually. What should it establish?

options.text: Design tokens for shared color values and semantic roles
More one-off styles
A screenshot folder
A rule that every designer picks a favorite purple

why: Design tokens store reusable design decisions such as color, spacing and typography values. Semantic tokens make consistent changes easier across a product.
takeaway: Design tokens: store reusable design decisions instead of repeating raw values.

question: A desktop dashboard uses a four-column data table. On a narrow phone, the columns become unreadable. What is the best response?

options.text: Shrink every text label until all columns fit
Adapt the layout for the smaller screen, prioritizing key information and suitable mobile patterns
Keep the desktop layout unchanged
Remove all data from mobile

why: Responsive design adapts content and interaction to the available space and context. It is not simply scaling a desktop layout down.
takeaway: Responsive design: adapt the experience to the screen, not just the dimensions.

question: A dashboard marks overdue tasks in red and completed tasks in green. Some users cannot distinguish the colors. What should be added?

options.text: More shades of red and green only
Text labels or icons so status is not communicated by color alone
Smaller labels
Remove status information entirely

why: Color should not be the only way information is conveyed. Additional labels, symbols or patterns make status perceivable to more people.
takeaway: Redundant encoding: communicate important meaning in more than one visual way.

question: A design system has separate button components for every color and size combination. Updates are becoming inconsistent. What is a better model?

options.text: Create a reusable button component with clearly defined variants and states
Duplicate every button on every screen
Stop documenting button behavior
Use screenshots instead of components

why: A component with controlled variants and states provides reuse while allowing legitimate differences, such as primary, secondary, disabled and loading.
takeaway: Component variants: reuse a reliable base while documenting meaningful differences.

question: A modal dialog opens, but keyboard users can still tab through links behind it. What should the team fix?

options.text: Trap focus appropriately within the modal while it is open, and return focus when it closes
Remove the close button
Make the modal open only on hover
Hide the visible focus indicator

why: A modal dialog should manage keyboard focus so users can interact with its content without accidentally moving behind it. Focus should return to the invoking control when appropriate.
takeaway: Focus management: keep keyboard navigation in the active task context.

question: A product uses pale gray text on a white background for important instructions. Some users struggle to read it. What should be checked first?

options.text: Whether the font is decorative
Text and background contrast against accessibility requirements
Whether the page has enough animations
Whether the text is centered

why: Insufficient contrast can make text difficult to perceive. Check the actual foreground and background contrast and adjust the colors while preserving the intended visual hierarchy.
takeaway: Contrast check: visual subtlety should not come at the cost of readability.

question: A sign-up form uses placeholder text as the only label for each input. Once users start typing, the hints disappear. What is the better pattern?

options.text: Keep a persistent visible label associated with each input
Remove all labels
Use a different placeholder color for every field
Put all field names in the page footer

why: Persistent labels remain available while users enter data and provide a reliable name for assistive technologies when correctly associated with inputs.
takeaway: Persistent labels: do not make users rely on disappearing hints to understand a field.

question: Users frequently miss a tiny close icon in a mobile dialog. What should the designer consider?

options.text: Increase the interactive target area and provide enough separation from nearby controls
Make the icon thinner
Move it closer to other small icons
Remove the accessible name

why: Larger, well-spaced touch targets are easier to activate, especially for users with motor impairments or when using a device one-handed.
takeaway: Touch target: design for fingers and real-world conditions, not just the visible icon.

question: An automated accessibility checker reports no serious issues. Can the team conclude the flow is accessible?

options.text: Yes, automated tools detect every accessibility problem
No. Combine automated checks with keyboard, assistive-technology and user testing
Yes, if the design uses a popular font
No. Automated tools should never be used

why: Automated tools catch many detectable issues but cannot evaluate every aspect of understanding, task completion or assistive-technology behavior.
takeaway: Accessibility is a practice: automate what you can and test the experience with people.

question: A major customer asks for a customizable dashboard. Interviews reveal that their real difficulty is finding two critical reports quickly. What should the product designer do?

options.text: Build the customizable dashboard exactly as requested
Explore the report-finding problem and test simpler ways to make those reports easier to access
Reject the request without investigation
Add every report to the home screen

why: Feature requests are clues, not complete requirements. Understanding the underlying job may reveal a simpler solution that serves more users.
takeaway: Reframe the request: solve the user problem, not automatically the suggested feature.

question: A startup wants to test whether local stores will accept online reservations. Which option is the best MVP approach?

options.text: Build a complete marketplace with loyalty, reviews and recommendations
Test the core reservation journey with a small number of stores and customers
Spend the entire budget polishing the logo
Wait until every possible feature is specified

why: A Minimum Viable Product is the smallest useful product or experiment that can test an important assumption and generate learning. It is not simply the smallest number of features.
takeaway: MVP: minimize the build while maximizing validated learning.

question: Your team has capacity for one improvement. Option A is requested by one executive but has little evidence. Option B addresses a frequent user problem and is aligned with the product goal. What should guide the decision?

options.text: Seniority of the person requesting the feature
Evidence of user impact, strategic alignment, effort and risk
Which option has the more exciting name
Whichever option is easiest to present

why: Prioritization should make trade-offs explicit. User impact, strategy, confidence, effort and risk provide a stronger basis than hierarchy or enthusiasm alone.
takeaway: Prioritization is a trade-off: compare value, evidence, effort and strategic fit.

question: Users love a proposed service and find it easy to use. However, each transaction costs the company more to deliver than it earns. Which product risk is most clearly unresolved?

options.text: Usability risk
Value risk
Business viability risk
Visual design risk

why: Viability asks whether the solution can work for the business, including its economics and operating model. Strong desirability and usability do not guarantee sustainable value.
takeaway: Product viability: a product must create value in a way the business can sustain.

question: A product team has a goal to increase successful first-week activation. They have already collected several user pain points and possible features. What structure can help connect the outcome to opportunities, solutions and experiments?

options.text: Opportunity Solution Tree
A mood board
A site map alone
A list of engineering estimates

why: An Opportunity Solution Tree connects a desired outcome to customer opportunities, possible solutions and experiments. It helps teams avoid jumping straight from a metric to a feature.
takeaway: Opportunity Solution Tree: connect outcomes to customer needs, solutions and tests.

question: A redesigned checkout increases the number of users who click "Pay," but payment failures also rise. What should the team do?

options.text: Declare success based on button clicks
Review the primary outcome together with guardrail metrics such as successful payments and errors
Hide the payment-failure metric
Stop measuring checkout performance

why: A guardrail metric helps detect negative side effects while optimizing a primary outcome. Clicks alone do not prove that users completed a successful purchase.
takeaway: Guardrail metrics: improve one outcome without quietly damaging another.

question: Many users start a subscription flow, but few reach the confirmation screen. You need to identify the step with the biggest loss. What should you examine?

options.text: A step-by-step conversion funnel, segmented where useful
The company logo engagement rate
The total number of app downloads only
The average screen brightness

why: Funnel analysis measures movement through a sequence of steps and helps identify where users drop off. Segmentation can reveal whether the issue affects particular devices or user groups.
takeaway: Funnel analysis: find where progress breaks down, then investigate why.

question: An A/B test has run for one day and version B is briefly ahead. The sample is small and weekday behavior may differ. What is the best next step?

options.text: Ship B immediately
Continue according to a pre-defined test plan until there is enough reliable evidence, while monitoring guardrails
Change the test variants every few hours
Stop the test because the first result is exciting

why: Early fluctuations in a small sample can be misleading. A sound experiment uses a planned duration or stopping rule, adequate evidence and relevant guardrail checks.
takeaway: Experiment discipline: decide how you will judge the test before looking for a winner.

question: A collaboration app wants a metric that reflects the core value users receive. Which is the best starting point for a North Star Metric?

options.text: Number of times the logo is displayed
Number of meaningful projects that teams successfully complete using the product
Total number of color themes available
Number of internal meetings held by the company

why: A North Star Metric should represent the value delivered to customers and connect to sustainable product growth. The exact metric depends on the product's value proposition.
takeaway: North Star Metric: measure value received, not activity that merely looks impressive.

question: A fitness app has many new sign-ups, but the team wants to know whether users return in the weeks after joining. Which analysis is most useful?

options.text: Retention cohorts grouped by sign-up period
A count of all downloads since launch
The number of buttons on the home screen
The total size of the app store listing

why: Cohort retention tracks groups of users over time, helping the team see whether people continue to return after first using the product.
takeaway: Cohort analysis: compare how groups behave over time, not just totals.

question: An engineer says a proposed animation will be expensive and may slow down older devices. What is the best response from the designer?

options.text: Insist that the mockup must be implemented exactly
Understand the user purpose, explore lighter alternatives and agree on an acceptable experience with engineering
Remove all motion without discussion
Ask the stakeholder to overrule engineering

why: Design and engineering should collaborate on the outcome and constraints. A simpler implementation may preserve the user benefit with lower performance or delivery cost.
takeaway: Collaborative feasibility: protect the user outcome while adapting the implementation.

question: A developer receives a polished screen but is unsure how loading, error, disabled and success states should behave. What should the designer provide?

options.text: Only a higher-resolution screenshot
Component states, interaction behavior, edge cases and relevant responsive rules
A link to an unrelated inspiration board
A note saying "use your judgment"

why: A useful handoff communicates behavior and edge cases, not just appearance. Shared components and clear acceptance criteria reduce implementation ambiguity.
takeaway: Design handoff: specify states and behavior, not only the happy-path screen.

question: In a release candidate, the primary button wraps onto two lines on a supported small phone and overlaps nearby text. What should the designer do?

options.text: Ignore it because the desktop version is correct
Reproduce the issue, document the device and conditions, assess severity and work with engineering on a fix
Change the design system without checking other screens
Ask users to rotate their phones permanently

why: Design QA checks the implemented experience against intended behavior across supported contexts. Clear reproduction details help the team resolve the issue efficiently.
takeaway: Design QA: verify the real build across the conditions users actually experience.

question: A stakeholder says, "Make the primary button green. Green feels more trustworthy." There is no evidence yet that color is the issue. What should the designer do?

options.text: Change it immediately because the stakeholder is senior
Clarify the goal, share relevant evidence and test the hypothesis if the decision matters
Refuse every visual suggestion
Add green to every component

why: A design critique should connect opinions to user needs, product goals and evidence. A stakeholder hypothesis can be tested without treating preference as proof.
takeaway: Evidence-led critique: turn opinions into hypotheses that can be examined.

question: A launch date is fixed and the team must reduce scope. Which approach best protects the product experience?

options.text: Remove random screens until the project fits
Protect the core user journey and essential states, then defer lower-value enhancements
Keep every feature but remove usability testing
Ship incomplete payment and error flows

why: Scope reduction should preserve the product's essential value and safe completion of core tasks. Lower-priority enhancements can be staged for later releases.
takeaway: Scope the release around the core journey, not around a random feature count.

question: A subscription app makes signing up easy but hides cancellation under several confusing menus. What is the most responsible design response?

options.text: Make cancellation equally clear and reasonably easy to find
Add more steps to discourage cancellation
Rename cancellation as an unrelated settings option
Use guilt-based messages to stop users leaving

why: A design should not manipulate users into staying. Clear, accessible cancellation supports user autonomy and trust.
takeaway: Avoid dark patterns: do not use interface friction to undermine informed choice.

question: A photo-editing app asks for camera access immediately on launch, before the user tries to take a photo. What is a better approach?

options.text: Ask at the moment the user tries to use the camera and explain why access is needed
Ask for every permission at first launch
Hide the purpose of the permission request
Block the entire app until every permission is granted

why: Contextual permission requests explain the value at the moment it is relevant. This supports informed choice and can improve comprehension.
takeaway: Just-in-time permission: ask when needed and explain the benefit clearly.

question: An AI assistant recommends a financial action, but its confidence is low and the user could lose money. What should the product do?

options.text: Present the recommendation as certain to encourage action
Communicate uncertainty and limitations, provide relevant context and keep the user in control of the decision
Hide that AI generated the recommendation
Automatically execute the action without confirmation

why: High-impact recommendations need appropriate transparency, uncertainty communication and user control. The interface should not imply confidence that the system does not have.
takeaway: Responsible AI: make limitations visible and preserve meaningful human control.

question: A simple event-booking app asks for a user's exact date of birth, home address and employer, even though none is needed to book a ticket. What should the designer recommend?

options.text: Collect everything in case it becomes useful later
Collect only the data needed for a clear purpose and explain that purpose to users
Make all fields mandatory
Hide the data collection in the terms page

why: Data minimization limits collection to what is necessary for the stated purpose. Less unnecessary data reduces privacy risk and builds trust.
takeaway: Data minimization: if the product does not need the data, do not collect it.

question: An AI assistant drafts a message to a customer and can send it automatically. The message may include pricing and delivery commitments. What is the safer interaction?

options.text: Send every generated message immediately
Show the draft, highlight important details and ask the user to review and confirm before sending
Hide the generated text after creation
Remove the ability to edit the message

why: When an AI action can create a meaningful external consequence, review and confirmation give people a chance to catch errors and retain control.
takeaway: Human-in-the-loop: keep people involved when automated actions have real consequences.
